results.result: Curtaining propensity was systematically evaluated across four plasma gases (argon, xenon, nitrogen, oxygen) at different ion currents and voltages. Argon and xenon produced the smoothest surfaces with curtaining propensity under 10% at low currents (~0.2 nA), while nitrogen and oxygen exhibited greater curtaining. Argon showed lower curtaining than xenon at higher currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 provide comprehensive experimental data on curtaining assessment with quantitative measurements across multiple conditions. The systematic comparison includes appropriate controls (different gases, currents, voltages) and quantitative scoring. The trend analysis and exceptions (e.g., nitrogen at 20 kV) are clearly documented with figure references.

results.result: Beam profiles of four plasma gases were characterized by measuring full width half maximum (FWHM) at different currents and voltages. Plasma sources showed considerably larger probe sizes than Ga-based sources. At 30 kV, argon had the smallest probe size, while at 20 kV all gases showed similar spot sizes with different plateau behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 describe systematic beam characterization with quantitative FWHM measurements. The comparison to Ga-based sources (C48) provides important context supported by citation. The voltage-dependent differences are clearly documented, though the biological implications of these differences could be better explored.

results.result: Imaging at 90° to the milled surface significantly improved image quality compared to 52° imaging. Resolution improved from 76±19 nm (52°) to 47±7 nm (90°), with immediately visible contrast enhancement. The improvement is attributed to differences in electron collection efficiency, which is maximal when normal to the SEM.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C83 demonstrate clear improvement in imaging quality with quantitative resolution measurements using FRC analysis. The physical explanation (electron collection efficiency, C83) is supported by citation. Visual observations are corroborated by quantitative metrics. The requirement for stage movement (C75) and its minimal impact on drift (addressed in C84-C87) strengthen the result.

results.result: Stage movement for 90° imaging introduces minimal drift. XY shift increased from 52±38 nm (no movement) to 96±71 nm (with movement), representing <1% of FOV. Z-drift remained minimal (48.1±1.4 nm vs 48.9±4 nm for 50 nm target), confirming the 50 nm milling step is achievable under cryogenic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 provide quantitative assessment of stage movement effects with appropriate error estimates. The measurements demonstrate that the twofold increase in XY drift is negligible in absolute terms. Z-drift measurements confirm milling accuracy. The conclusion that stage movement does not significantly compromise data quality is well-supported.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM of HeLa cells (500 slices, 50 nm depth) revealed various membranous compartments including nucleus, ER, mitochondria, and cristae. Two centrosomes with centriole pairs were observed, with spacing consistent with prophase (1.2 µm between centrosomes, 543 nm and 1561 nm between centriole pairs).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 describe detailed cellular observations with quantitative measurements. The centrosome spacing and centriole measurements are supported by citations (C60, C61, C62) confirming biological interpretation. The negative observation (C63, no spindle microtubules) is appropriately reported. The resolution achieved allows visualization of these structures.

results.result: Serial pFIB/SEM of HPF mouse brain cortex tissue (844.4 µm³ volume) revealed diverse cell types, myelinated neurons (diameter 0.53-2.8 µm), mitochondria with cristae (~87 total), and synaptic junctions with pre-synaptic vesicles (20-30 nm diameter). Synapse I contained ~184 vesicles, Synapse II ~98 vesicles, with diverse morphologies consistent with previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C73 demonstrate the technique's capability for tissue imaging with extensive quantitative data. The observations span multiple scales from tissue organization to nanometer-scale vesicles. Quantitative counts and measurements are provided. Comparison to prior work (C73) validates the biological observations. The diversity of structures observed demonstrates the method's versatility.

results.result: Plunge-frozen R. rubrum imaged without stain or fixative revealed minimal artefacts and clear visualization of lipid droplets, inner/outer membranes (30-80 nm apart), and both mature (30-60 nm diameter) and nascent chromatophores. In 8 segmented cells, 2772 mature and 84 nascent chromatophores were observed, with nascent forms unevenly distributed (one cell with ~12% nascent, most with few or none). Data collection was accomplished in 2.5 hr automated.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C103 demonstrate successful imaging of bacteria with quantitative analysis. The observation of nascent chromatophores budding from inner membrane (C98) is novel (C97). Quantitative segmentation data (C99) with extrapolation (C100) is reasonable. The uneven distribution observation (C101-C102) is biologically interesting and demonstrates the technique's ability to capture rare events (C103). Measurements are consistent with cited literature (C93, C96).

results.result: Vero cells milled with nitrogen plasma (worst performing gas) still revealed subcellular structures including 138 NPCs, mitochondrial networks, and membrane contact sites. Despite severe limitations (46 slices vs 500 for HeLa, 7 failed attempts), quantification showed 26 LD-ER contacts and 48 mitochondria-ER MCS with similar volumes (1-5 × 10⁻³ µm³) and Gaussian distribution, suggesting limits in ER tracking of organelles.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C114 demonstrate that even the worst-performing gas can yield useful biological insights, though with significant technical challenges (C106-C107). The quantitative analysis of membrane contact sites (C111-C113) provides novel biological insight. The interpretation about ER tracking limits (C114) is reasonable but speculative. The high failure rate and limited slice number indicate this is not the optimal approach but validates the robustness of the biological observations.

results.result: Fixed (4% paraformaldehyde) mouse heart tissue imaged by serial pFIB/SEM revealed sarcomeres (average length 1.68 µm) with visible Z-disc, I-band, A-bands, and putative M-line, organized between mitochondrial columns. The volume (2698.4 µm³) contained 997 mitochondria, giving a concentration of 0.36 mitochondria/µm³, consistent with previous observations in mouse heart.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C124 demonstrate application to fixed tissue with detailed structural observations. The sarcomere length measurement (C119) is quantitative with appropriate statistics (SD, N). The mitochondrial concentration (C123) agrees with prior literature (C124), validating the quantitative analysis. The use of fixation (C116) is justified for practical reasons. The detailed visualization of sarcomere components (C118) demonstrates resolution capability.

results.result: FRC-based resolution assessment across datasets showed sample-dependent variation (brain vs HeLa despite identical parameters; R. rubrum vs Vero twofold difference) reflecting importance of focusing, astigmatism, and sample variability. No resolution degradation was observed during acquisition series, even in long runs (500 slices).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 provide systematic resolution assessment across multiple samples. The observation of sample-dependent variation (C126-C127) is important for understanding technique limitations. The lack of resolution degradation over time (C128) demonstrates stability. However, the FRC method's calibration and patch size choices could affect absolute values. The comparative analysis is more robust than absolute resolution claims.

results.result: Lamellae of R. rubrum and RPE-1 cells were prepared using serial pFIB/SEM (200 pA) followed by final polishing (60 pA) and imaged by both SEM and TEM. Features could be correlated between modalities despite physical differences arising from imaging depth (SEM: ~25 nm surface, TEM: entire 300 nm thickness). Fluorescence from chlorophyll was correlated with both pFIB/SEM and TEM images.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C138 demonstrate compatibility with downstream cryo-ET workflows. The correlation between SEM and TEM (C131, C136) validates the approach. The explanation of differences (C132-C135) based on imaging physics is sound. The multimodal correlation including fluorescence (C137) is particularly valuable. The conclusion (C138) that serial pFIB/SEM is suitable for correlative workflows is well-supported, though potential ion damage effects are not fully addressed here.

results.result: Charging artefacts, occurring in lipid-rich regions and manifesting as dark spots with asymmetric streaks, were computationally mitigated using U-Net segmentation of charge centers followed by row-by-row filtering. Automated segmentation achieved 0.93 Dice coefficient compared to manual cleanup, indicating minimal manual intervention needed. Overall image resolution remained unchanged after charge removal.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C146 describe a practical solution to a significant technical challenge. The physical basis for charging (C139) is established. The computational approach (C142-C143) is clearly described with quantitative validation (C144). The high Dice coefficient (C144) supports the claim of minimal manual intervention (C145). The preservation of resolution (C146) is important. However, the method cannot recover information in the charged region itself, which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Automated segmentation of mitochondria in heart tissue using SuRVos2 achieved 0.87 Dice score compared to manual segmentation, with volume percentages in agreement (24% automated vs 20% manual). Component counts differed (15 automated vs 23 manual after filtering), demonstrating feasibility of automated segmentation but requiring additional work to quantify errors.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C151 demonstrate proof-of-concept for automated analysis. The Dice score (C148) indicates good agreement. The volume percentage agreement (C149) is encouraging. The discrepancy in component counts (C150) is honestly reported and highlights remaining challenges. The conclusion (C151) appropriately characterizes this as a baseline demonstration rather than a fully validated method. Additional validation would strengthen this result.

results.result: All four gases (O, N, Ar, Xe) can produce smooth surfaces under some conditions, with behavior depending on ion current and voltage. Monatomic gases (Ar, Xe) are speculated to be less reactive and less prone to curtaining. Argon was selected as optimal for automated procedures based on low curtaining at low current and better performance at high currents, despite diatomic gases showing high automation failure rates (>80% vs <10% for argon).
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C164 synthesize the gas comparison results into practical recommendations. The observation that all gases can work under some conditions (C156) is important. The speculation about monatomic gases (C158) is clearly identified as such. The selection of argon (C164) is well-justified by the data. The quantitative comparison of failure rates (C162) strongly supports the choice. The discussion of prior work with oxygen (C163) provides context.

results.result: Prior work showed Ar plasma (30 kV, 60 pA) adversely affected ribosome resolution within ~45 nm of surface despite smooth surfaces, attributed to ion damage. For serial pFIB/SEM, argon wattage is twofold higher (200 pA at 20 kV vs 60 pA at 30 kV). Nitrogen showed higher resolution than argon in comparative imaging, suggesting damage may depend on plasma type and not simply correlate with curtaining, but further investigation is required.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C171 raise important concerns about potential damage but lack direct experimental validation in this study. The citation of prior work (C165-C167) is appropriate. The inference about lack of correlation between curtaining and damage (C168) is logical. The observation that nitrogen showed higher resolution than argon (C170) is intriguing but based on limited comparison. The speculation (C171) is appropriately cautious. This represents an important limitation requiring future work.

results.result: SEM imaging dose was under 10⁻² e⁻/Å² over the whole scanned image, lower than cryo-ET imaging doses. SEM-induced damage would be expected to be confined to the interaction depth (<50 nm), contained within the same volume as FIB damage (~45 nm near the surface).
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C174 provide important dosimetry information. The comparison to cryo-ET doses (C173) with citation provides context. The inference about damage localization (C174) is reasonable based on electron interaction physics and supported by citation. However, this is theoretical expectation rather than direct measurement of damage in this study. The low dose is reassuring for the technique's viability.

results.result: Cryo-serial pFIB/SEM enables mesoscale imaging (10 nm to 10 µm) of vitrified samples while maintaining hydration shells for downstream structural biology. Despite challenges of low contrast, curtaining, and charging, an automated workflow produced 3D volumes of bacteria, cells, and tissue with 20-50 nm resolution. The approach is highly controllable, relatively rapid, laboratory-based, and compatible with subsequent imaging modalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C29-C32, and C175-C178 represent the overarching conclusions of the study. The technical challenges (C3) were systematically addressed through the work. The resolution achievement (C4) is supported by multiple datasets. The range of samples (C32) demonstrates versatility. The advantages listed (C178) are supported by the experimental results. The conclusion that this is a useful addition to structural biology (C175-C176) is well-justified by the comprehensive demonstration across multiple biological systems.

results.result: Background and motivation: Current FIB/SEM is almost exclusively applied to fixed, stained samples. Cryo-ET requires thin lamellae (<300 nm) typically prepared with Ga+ FIB. Current targeting approaches (cryo-CLEM, soft X-ray tomography) have limitations. Plasma FIB offers higher currents than Ga+ for faster ablation. Biological SEM imaging is challenging due to low contrast from light atoms, traditionally addressed by fixation/staining which precludes near-atomic resolution analysis. Imaging at crossover energies can reduce charging.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C28 establish the context and rationale for the study. These are primarily literature-based knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations. The identification of technical challenges (C3, C12, C21-C23) and limitations of existing approaches (C13, C15-C16, C25-C26) clearly motivates the development of cryo-serial pFIB/SEM. The technical background on plasma FIB (C18-C20) and SEM physics (C27-C28) is accurate.

results.result: Initial imaging parameters were established: 52° SEM angle, 50 nm milling step (compromise between workflow and electron interaction depth of 30-90 nm), imaging at 1.1-1.2 kV with 6.3-13 pA current, 100 ns dwell time with 50-100 line integration. Depth of field was ~20 µm at both 1 and 2 kV, requiring focus correction after ~400 slices at 50 nm step thickness.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 and C89-C90 describe methodological optimization with clear rationale. The milling step choice (C52) balances practical and physical considerations based on cited literature (C53-C54). The imaging parameters (C55-C56) are empirically optimized. The depth of field measurement (C89) with practical implication (C90) is useful for experimental planning. These represent important technical details for reproducibility.

results.result: The authors assessed curtaining propensity across four plasma gases (argon, xenon, nitrogen, oxygen) at different currents and voltages. They found that argon and xenon produce the smoothest surfaces with curtaining propensity under 10% at low currents, while nitrogen and oxygen exhibit greater curtaining. Argon showed lower curtaining than xenon at higher currents.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested additional data on curtaining behavior over time during serial imaging sessions (Essential revision 2), noting that the current assessment was done on individual milled windows. The manuscript does not show temporal accumulation of curtains during automated runs, which is critical for evaluating the technique's performance in actual imaging workflows.

results.result: The authors characterized beam profiles of four plasma gases by measuring full width half maximum at different currents and voltages. Plasma sources showed considerably larger probe sizes than Ga-based sources, with argon having the smallest probe size at 30 kV.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly requested additional data on milling resolution and beam cross-sections (Essential revision 3), stating 'No detail about the milling resolution has been reported' and noting that different beam cross-sections are expected to affect z-resolution. The provided beam profile data does not fully address how this impacts actual milling performance.

results.result: The authors explored imaging at 90° to the milled surface versus the default 52° angle. They found that 90° imaging provided improved contrast and resolution (47±7 nm vs 76±19 nm), with features like bacterial outer membranes being more prominently visible.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised multiple concerns about this result: they requested comments on collection efficiency effects (Essential revision 4), explanation of resolution loss upon tilting (Essential revision 5), and noted potential suboptimal astigmatism correction affecting the comparison (Essential revision 6). Reviewer 1 specifically questioned the contrast improvement mechanism, noting that secondary electron generation should increase with tilt for both features and background, making the observed contrast difference unexpected.

results.result: The authors identified charging artifacts as a limitation of cryo-serial pFIB/SEM and developed a computational approach using U-Net neural networks to remove these artifacts. The automated segmentation achieved a 0.93 Dice coefficient score compared to manual cleanup.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated that 'the paper does not show or discuss how plasma beams can mitigate charging artifacts (or not)' and requested comparison of charging artifacts with different sources including Gallium before computational correction (Essential revision 1). The manuscript only addresses computational correction, not whether plasma beams inherently reduce charging compared to other sources.

results.result: The authors imaged 500 slices of plunge-frozen HeLa cells and visualized various organelles including nucleus, ER, mitochondria, and two centrosomes. They measured centrosome spacing (1.2 µm center-to-center) and centriole spacing (543 nm and 1561 nm), consistent with prophase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about these cellular observations. The public review notes the work 'should be very useful for addressing many biological questions,' implicitly accepting the demonstrated capability to visualize subcellular structures.

results.result: The authors imaged mouse brain cortical tissue (844.4 µm³ volume) and observed various cell types, myelinated neurons, mitochondria, and synapses. They quantified synaptic vesicles (~184 in Synapse I, ~98 in Synapse II) and observed diverse synapse morphologies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these specific observations from brain tissue. The public review acknowledges the work demonstrates 'subcellular architecture at sufficient contrast for ultrastructural analyses,' supporting the validity of these findings.

results.result: The authors imaged plunge-frozen R. rubrum bacteria and observed both developing and mature chromatophores. They identified nascent chromatophores budding from the inner membrane and quantified 2772 mature and 84 nascent chromatophores in eight segmented cells, noting uneven distribution across the population.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these bacterial observations. The demonstration of rare events like chromatophore budding aligns with the reviewers' recognition that the approach 'should be very useful for addressing many biological questions.'

results.result: The authors characterized Vero cells imaged with nitrogen plasma, identifying 138 nuclear pore complexes and quantifying the mitochondrial network, ER, and lipid droplets. They identified 26 LD-to-ER contacts and 48 mitochondria-to-ER membrane contact sites with similar volume distributions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these specific quantitative observations. However, the context is that this dataset was acquired with nitrogen (the worst-performing gas) after seven failed attempts, demonstrating technical challenges rather than optimal performance.

results.result: The authors imaged fixed heart tissue and visualized sarcomeres with Z-disc, I-band, A-bands, and putative M-line. They measured average sarcomere length (1.68 µm) and quantified 997 mitochondria in the volume, yielding a concentration of 0.36 mitochondria/µm³ consistent with previous studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these heart tissue observations. The agreement with previous literature on mitochondrial content supports the validity of the quantitative measurements.

results.result: The authors used FRC to assess resolution across datasets, finding typical resolution of 20-50 nm. They observed differences between samples reflecting the importance of focusing, astigmatism, and sample variability, but found no evidence of resolution degradation during data collection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that 'the resolution measurements presented in the last supplementary figures do not relate to the use of plasma FIB/SEM in comparison with other beams' (Essential revision 1). The resolution assessment does not demonstrate advantages of plasma FIB over other ion sources, which is a key claim of the manuscript.

results.result: The authors generated lamellae of R. rubrum and RPE-1 cells and demonstrated correlation between SEM images during fabrication and TEM images after fabrication. They showed it was possible to correlate subcellular structures and fluorescence from chlorophyll with both pFIB/SEM and TEM images.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested demonstration that 'features detected in the SEM can be used to target areas of interest for cryo-ET' and whether 'structural preservation in the cryo-ET reconstructions' can be shown (Essential revision 7). Reviewer 2 specifically noted disappointment that downstream cryo-ET targeting effectiveness is not demonstrated, suggesting authors either provide proof-of-concept data or explicitly state this is future work.

results.result: The authors demonstrated automated segmentation of mitochondria in heart tissue using SuRVos2, achieving a Dice score of 0.87 compared to manual segmentation. However, component counts differed (15 automated vs 23 manual), indicating some discrepancies.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly suggested applying 'an automated segmentation algorithm to their volumetric data as a more unbiased and practical metric to evaluate the degree to which cryo-FIB/SEM imaging increases resolution, contrast, and interpretability of subcellular features at scale.' The reviewers also asked whether 'automated segmentation approaches be applied to the FIB/SEM volumes in similar ways to cryo-ET reconstructions' (Essential revision 7). While the authors provide some segmentation results, the discrepancy in counts and limited scope suggest this needs further development.

results.result: The authors concluded that all four gases can produce smooth surfaces under some conditions, with argon selected as optimal for automated procedures on vitrified samples. They speculate that monatomic gases are less reactive and less prone to curtaining.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the comparative evaluation of gases and the selection of argon, as evidenced by the public review stating the work 'concluding that one of the four plasma sources tested produces the highest quality images.' The speculation about monatomic gases is appropriately identified as such in the manuscript.

results.result: The authors discussed potential damage from plasma FIB milling, noting that prior work showed argon plasma affected ribosome resolution within ~45 nm of the surface. They compared their higher wattage conditions to lamella polishing and discussed SEM dose being lower than cryo-ET, with damage expected to be confined to <50 nm depth.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this discussion of potential damage mechanisms. The authors appropriately cite prior work and acknowledge uncertainties, noting that 'further investigation is required' regarding the relationship between plasma type, current, and damage.

results.result: The authors claim that cryo-serial pFIB/SEM enables mesoscale imaging (10 nm to 10 µm) of vitrified samples, is a useful addition to the structural biology toolbox, and can generate 3D maps suitable for targeting while maintaining hydration shells for downstream structural biology. They achieved 20-50 nm resolution across bacteria, cells, and tissue.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the work is 'important' and 'timely,' they raised fundamental questions about whether the approach is effective for downstream targeting (Essential revision 7). Reviewer 2 noted readers will 'come up somewhat disappointed that this is not demonstrated' and suggested the manuscript should 'more explicitly state upfront' whether this is solely focused on volumetric imaging or includes targeting validation. The claim about suitability for targeting remains unproven.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate curtaining assessment (C37-C45). OpenEval finds the systematic comparison with quantitative measurements SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, requesting additional data on curtaining behavior over time during serial imaging sessions, noting current assessment was only on individual milled windows.

Both evaluate beam characterization (C46-C50). OpenEval finds systematic FWHM measurements SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, explicitly requesting additional data on milling resolution and beam cross-sections, stating 'No detail about the milling resolution has been reported.'

Both evaluate imaging quality improvement with tilted stage (C74-C83). OpenEval finds clear improvement with quantitative FRC analysis SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about collection efficiency effects, resolution loss upon tilting, suboptimal astigmatism correction, and questioning the contrast improvement mechanism.

Both address charging artifacts (C3, C139-C146). OpenEval finds the computational correction approach SUPPORTED with high Dice coefficient. Peer reviewers rate it UNSUPPORTED, stating the paper does not show whether plasma beams inherently mitigate charging compared to other sources like Gallium before computational correction.

Both evaluate cellular observations (C57-C63). OpenEval finds detailed quantitative measurements with appropriate citations SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, with no specific concerns raised and implicit acceptance of demonstrated subcellular visualization capability.

Both evaluate brain tissue imaging (C64-C73). OpenEval finds extensive quantitative data demonstrating versatility SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, acknowledging the work demonstrates subcellular architecture at sufficient contrast for ultrastructural analyses.

Both evaluate bacterial imaging (C91-C103). OpenEval finds novel observations with quantitative analysis SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, with no concerns raised about these observations, aligning with recognition that the approach is useful for biological questions.

Both evaluate nitrogen gas results with membrane contact site analysis (C104-C114 for OpenEval, C109-C114 for peer). OpenEval finds useful biological insights despite technical challenges SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate the specific quantitative observations (C109-C114) SUPPORTED, though context shows this was worst-performing gas with high failure rate.

Both evaluate fixed heart tissue observations (C115-C124 for OpenEval, C117-C124 for peer). OpenEval finds detailed structural observations with quantitative validation SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, with no concerns raised and agreement with previous literature supporting validity.

Both evaluate resolution assessment (C125-C128). OpenEval finds systematic assessment with sample-dependent variation SUPPORTED, noting comparative analysis is more robust than absolute claims. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, stating resolution measurements do not demonstrate advantages of plasma FIB over other ion sources.

Both evaluate compatibility with cryo-ET workflows (C129-C138 for OpenEval, C129, C131-C138 for peer). OpenEval finds multimodal correlation well-SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, requesting demonstration that SEM features can effectively target cryo-ET and proof of structural preservation, noting disappointment this is not shown.

Both evaluate automated segmentation (C147-C151). OpenEval finds proof-of-concept SUPPORTED but notes discrepancies and characterizes it as baseline demonstration. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, suggesting automated segmentation as more unbiased metric and questioning whether approaches can be applied similarly to cryo-ET reconstructions.

Both evaluate gas comparison and argon selection (C156-C164 for OpenEval, C156-C160, C164 for peer). OpenEval finds practical recommendations well-justified by data SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, accepting comparative evaluation and argon selection as producing highest quality images.

Both address potential damage concerns (C165-C171 for OpenEval, C166-C174 for peer). OpenEval rates it UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct experimental validation in this study. Peer reviewers rate it SUPPORTED, accepting the discussion of damage mechanisms with appropriate citations and acknowledgment of uncertainties.

OpenEval evaluates dosimetry information (C172-C174) as SUPPORTED with appropriate context. Peer R14 includes these claims in broader damage discussion (C166-C174) rated SUPPORTED. Both accept the theoretical expectations about damage localization, though OpenEval notes this is expectation rather than direct measurement.

Both evaluate overarching conclusions (C1-C4, C29-C32, C175-C178). OpenEval finds comprehensive demonstration justifies conclusions as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, acknowledging work is important and timely but raising fundamental questions about effectiveness for downstream targeting, suggesting manuscript should more explicitly state scope upfront.

OpenEval evaluates stage movement effects (C84-C88) as SUPPORTED with quantitative assessment showing negligible impact. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific claims.

OpenEval evaluates context and rationale claims (C5-C28) as SUPPORTED, noting literature-based knowledge with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these background claims.

OpenEval evaluates methodological optimization (C51-C56, C89-C90) as SUPPORTED with clear rationale for parameter choices. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these technical details.
